title: Pluggable expert handshake timing - case notes
content:
Summary:

This note documents an experiment-driven investigation into a recurring class of p50/p99 latency spikes we observed on MoE-enabled endpoints when servicing long-context requests across Llama, Mistral and Qwen model variants. The pattern is distinct from pure KV-eviction or kernel contention: it centers on the timing and coordination of the "expert handshake" — the sequence from gate-selection to expert prefetch + readiness to token fanout.

Why this matters:
- Spikes typically appear at mid-to-long token positions (200+ tokens) and disproportionately impact p99 while leaving p50 mostly unchanged.
- Affects correctness of latency SLOs for Dedicated customers with tight tail requirements.
- Traces suggest cross-model differences: Llama runs show more frequent short stalls, Mistral longer stalls with larger variance, Qwen sees fewer but much higher-amplitude instantaneous stalls.

Definitions / handshake phases we instrumented:
1) Gate compute (G): CPU/GPU op to compute gating logits and choose experts.
2) Routing encode (R): serialization + packetizing of indices/fanout for scheduler.
3) Prefetch request (P): issuing memory transfers and kernel warmup requests to the target expert worker.
4) Expert readiness / enqueue (E): expert is ready to execute and the token is enqueued.
5) Fanout reduction and join (F): gathering expert outputs back to the requesting session.

Hypothesis summary we tested:
- H1: Poorly-aligned prefetch windows cause a race where P completes either too early (eviction before use) or too late (expert idle-wait), creating variability.
- H2: Scheduler serialization combined with head-of-line gating bursts causes contention on the enqueue path (E) — especially for hot experts with high fanout.
- H3: Model-specific microkernel warmup (Qwen small-col kernels vs Mistral fused kernels) interacts with prefetch timing producing different stall modes.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Models: Llama-13B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-7B
- Context lengths: 128, 512, 2048 (main observations at 2048)
- Fanout profiles: uniform (2 experts), skewed-hot (1 expert gets 60% traffic), bursty session (stochastic gating with burst size 8)
- Prefetch windows: none, conservative (ahead 1 step), aggressive (ahead 8 steps), adaptive (timing feedback)
- Scheduler: single-threaded enqueue vs worker-pool with lock-free ring buffers

Key observations:
- Prefetch window tuning dominates impact on p99. Aggressive prefetch (ahead 8) reduces average stall frequency but increases single-event stall magnitude when eviction occurs (dramatic with Llama due to smaller token-memory locality).
- Adaptive prefetch that observes expert queue depth and runtime readiness performed best across models; it reduced p99 by ~18% vs our baseline for Mistral and ~12% for Llama. Qwen gained ~22% on p99 but showed a small increase in p50 under heavy bursty load.
- Scheduler serialization (a global enqueue lock) is the single biggest source of tail spikes when many sessions simultaneously try to enqueue to a hot expert. Replacing the lock with per-expert lock-free rings cut p99 for skewed-hot profile by 30-45% depending on model.
- Kernel warmup differences: Qwen’s microkernels have non-linear cold-start penalty (cold-first-run >10x single-step op), which explains the high amplitude but low-frequency spikes for Qwen. For Mistral fused kernels, the warmup is more gradual leading to longer sustained slowdowns.

Trace excerpts (timestamp ms relative to token emission):
- 0.0 G (gate) 
- 0.6 R (route serialize)
- 1.3 P (prefetch req issued)
- 1.8 P-complete (DMA in-flight)
- 1.9 E (enqueue attempt) -> blocked 12.7 ms (global enqueue lock)
- 14.6 E-complete
- 15.1 F (reduction)

Another trace (Qwen burst):
- 0.0 G
- 0.8 R
- 1.1 P issued
- 1.2 P-complete
- 1.3 E enqueue -> success
- 1.4 kernel cold start -> 45 ms first-run penalty
- 46.5 F

Root causes distilled:
- Congestion at enqueue path when many sessions target the same expert (hotspot). The contention pattern is aggravated by a global coordinator which serializes metadata writes.
- Prefetch window is a two-edged sword; misaligned windows either cause eviction churn (higher overall work) or late prefetch causing stalls.
- Model kernel warmup characteristics differ and interact with the enqueue & scheduling design. Qwen needs special handling for cold kernels.
- NUMA/PCIe topology matters: when the scheduler and the target expert worker are on different NUMA nodes / different GPU host bridges, we observed +10–25% additional enqueue latency.

Mitigations attempted and results:
- Per-expert lock-free ring buffers for enqueue: large win for skewed workloads. Reduced enqueue-block time by 60% median and p99 by 30–45% in skewed-hot tests.
- Adaptive prefetch controller: uses feedback from expert queue depth and recent enqueue latency to shrink/grow window. Best cross-model balance; safe default for Dedicated customers.
- Hot-expert backpressure: when an expert queue depth exceeds threshold, gate outputs are temporarily skewed to secondary experts (soft fallthrough). Reduced p99 violations but requires careful quality monitoring.
- Kernel warmup cache: keep a tiny persistent pool of warmed kernels per-worker for Qwen; reduces cold-start spikes but increases steady-state memory footprint. For Qwen reduced first-run penalty from ~45 ms to ~3 ms in our tests.
- NUMA affinity enforcement: pin coordinator and target expert workers to same NUMA domain when possible; improved stability but not always feasible for multi-tenant hosts.

Open follow-ups / TODOs:
- Add a cheap enqueue path micro-benchmark to CI that simulates skewed-hot workloads across different CPU/GPU topologies. (JIRA-RT-1445)
- Instrument and plot per-expert kernel cold-start counters in the Console (ops surface) so customers can see warmup noise per model. (product request)
- Explore hierarchical scheduler: lightweight fast-path for low-fanout enqueues, heavyweight path for large fanout sessions. Prototype in branch gh/handshake-fastpath.
- Evaluate interaction with KV-cache eviction heuristics; prefetch windows might need to be synchronized with KV lifetimes to avoid churn.

Practical recommendations (for ops and product):
- Default to adaptive prefetch for Dedicated clusters. Tune aggressive window only for throughput-first tenants after profiling.
- Deploy per-expert enqueue rings where host CPU counts > 24 and expected skew is high.
- For Qwen-heavy fleets, enable a small kernel warmup pool on hot workers; expose a runtime flag for memory footprint vs tail-latency tradeoff.
- Add per-region NUMA-aware placement heuristics to reduce cross-domain enqueue stalls.

Appendix: short config snippets tried (pseudocode):
- adaptive prefetch controller:
  - window = clamp(base + alpha * avg_enqueue_latency, min=1, max=16)
  - if expert_queue_depth > high_watermark -> window -= 1
  - if kernel_cold_count > threshold -> pre-warm kernel on next idle cycle

- soft fallthrough gating rule:
  - if target_expert_queue_depth > 0.8 * max_depth && fallback_available:
    - reroute portion p = min(0.25, (queue_depth/max_depth)-0.8) of tokens to fallback experts

Notes on reproducibility: all experiments ran on the Dedicated test cluster (4 hosts, A100s), workload generator seeded with deterministic gating RNG. Traces captured with trace-id prefix "ph-handshake-" and stored in /traces/handshake/2025-08.

Conclusions:
The "expert handshake" is a distributed coordination problem where timing windows, scheduling serialization, kernel warmup behavior and topology interact nonlinearly. There is no single silver bullet but a combination of per-expert enqueue fast-paths, adaptive prefetching, kernel warmup caches (for Qwen) and NUMA-aware placement significantly reduces p99 tail exposure while preserving throughput.

If we converge on the adaptive prefetch + per-expert ring approach we should schedule a canary rollout on a low-risk Dedicated pool for two weeks and capture tail coverage metrics before broader rollout.

Authors: Aisha Patel (owner), notes contributions from Diego Ramos and Lena Fischer.

End of note.
